claims.text: Q235 steel contains a small amount of manganese.
The as-received, unexposed Q235 steel has no preformed protective oxide scale.
In harsh oxygen-containing environments, manganese in Q235 steel preferentially oxidizes to form a thin, adherent Mn-oxide surface layer.
A Mn-oxide layer acts as a protective barrier that suppresses further corrosion of the iron matrix.
Elevated temperature accelerates manganese diffusion from the bulk to the steel surface.
Greater manganese mobility at elevated temperature promotes faster and more continuous formation of a protective Mn-oxide film than at room temperature.
Manganese has a lower Gibbs free energy of oxidation than the relevant competing iron-oxidation process and therefore oxidizes preferentially at corrosion onset.
The Mn-oxide film limits subsequent oxidation and dissolution of the underlying iron.
Samples that form a Mn-oxide film will have lower mass-loss rates than reference samples with minimal Mn oxidation.
Samples that form a Mn-oxide film will exhibit less iron dissolution than reference samples with minimal Mn oxidation.
Elevated-temperature samples are expected to show greater Mn-oxide surface enrichment and better corrosion resistance than room-temperature samples.
Lower temperature or inhibited manganese mobility produces less Mn oxidation and consequently higher corrosion rates and more extensive iron degradation.
The proposed protective mechanism requires sufficient oxygen for manganese oxidation.
Extreme chloride concentrations, strongly complexing agents, or severe oxygen limitation may reduce or eliminate the protective effect of the Mn-oxide film.
Q235 steel's low manganese content may limit the robustness of Mn-oxide film formation.
Competing corrosion pathways may outweigh any protective benefit from manganese.
Room-temperature and elevated-temperature exposures in controlled chloride-rich or acidic electrolytes can be compared using weight loss, XPS, SEM-EDS, and electrochemical measurements.
Failure to observe either temperature-dependent Mn-oxide formation or an association between Mn-oxide formation and improved corrosion resistance would falsify the proposed hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome refers to an 'untreated reference,' which could mean the initially unexposed steel, whereas the baseline is defined as steel exposed to the same corrosive environment but with minimal Mn oxidation. These are materially different reference states.
